description: We are a group of Computer Science students who believe in software capable of solving real-world problems. Education, the way we see it, is the key to a just society, so throughout our lives we have fought to enhance it. For this challenge, we managed to connect it with agriculture and data analysis. After all, we live in an interconnected world where contributing to the solution of a problem can, with enough creativity, help to answer another. That’s what we stand for.
summary: Weather Detective sits at the intersection of statistics, farming and education: a web platform for climate trend analysis where users can select any region in the world and explore preprocessed NASA data. It was built for farmers in Chihuahua, a region that has faced increasingly severe droughts and rising temperatures over recent decades. Even experienced farmers cannot observe the global climate variables that shape their harvests, and raw charts cannot tell whether a dry year is just a bad streak or part of a long-term trend, because climate data is noisy, seasonal and variable. Weather Detective fills that gap by measuring the size of each change with the Theil-Sen slope, testing whether it is real with the Mann-Kendall test (with the Hamed-Rao correction for autocorrelation), and mapping trends pixel by pixel with False Discovery Rate correction to avoid false positives. It is also an educational tool for a new generation: young people, who are often the most comfortable with digital tools, can use Weather Detective to read the data, build their own analytical skills, and grow more interested in the science behind the climate, while sharing what they learn in clear terms with their farming families. In this way, Weather Detective pursues two goals at once: developing the next generation’s capacity for data analysis, and supporting better, evidence-based decisions that help protect and improve harvests.
details:
What does it do?

Converts rough data from NASA datasets into visual data for trend identification, helping students and the public to investigate how the Earth system is changing.

  • Allows users to pick a climate variable (temperature, temperature, precipitation, humidity, wind, solar radiation, evapotranspiration, or soil moisture) and a place.
  • Shows raw monthly values and the deseasonalized trend.
  • Comparing different regions to visualize opposite trends in same variable.
  • Answers for what is changing, where, in what quantity, and whether or not the change would be statistically significant.
How does it work?

The web platform is fed NASA POWER Datasets, so that when the user selects a certain region and a variable, the next flow comes as it follows:

  1. Times series extracted for the selected area.
  2. Seasonal cycle is removed so that regular yearly swings aren't hidden by long term signal.
  3. Thein-Sein Slope: The trend is estimated by obtaining the rate of change.
  4. Mann-Kendall test: Test significance, reporting p-value and a confidence interval.
  5. Result traduction: The results are translated into natural language, stating the direction, the magnitude and whether the trend is statistically significant.
What benefits does it have?

Weather Detective enhances accesibility, as it contributes to the public being able to access the interpreted data from anywhere in the world. It also firmly stands with scientific rigor, as all data was properly cleansed for the statistical model (significance, slops) to work properly.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Farming families in Chihuahua make decisions about water, crops, and land every season, but the long-term climate evidence behind those decisions sits in technical datasets few people can read. Weather Detective opens that door, starting with agricultural youth. We aim to give young people from Chihuahua’s agricultural communities the tools to analyze trends in their own region’s data. By learning to tell a real trend from a bad year, they can bring evidence to conversations with their families about water, drought, and farming decisions.

The project also strengthens education and critical thinking. Students learn to ask whether a pattern is real or random, that “significant” is not the same as “important,” and that a trend does not prove its cause. Because the app reports non-significant results as clearly as significant ones, they practice weighing evidence and living with uncertainty, skills that matter well beyond science.

We will start with a pilot of workshops in agricultural technical high schools, supported by local government programs, and measure how many students complete them, what share can interpret a trend without help, and how many families they share it with. The platform will remain free and open to use.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project? 
  • Frontend: React, Vite, TypeScript, MapLibre GL, Plotly, pnpm.
  • Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, Pydantic, pymannkendall, uv.
  • Precomputed data: Python pipeline for demos and pixel trend maps, served as static files.
  • Architecture & Contracts: Pydantic models → OpenAPI → TypeScript types.
  • Quality and tooling: ruff, pytest, ESLint, Vitest, Pull requests with automated tests.
  • Deployment and infrastructure: Vercel, Render, Docker, GitHub.
  • AI-Assisted Development: omp (oh-my-pi), running Anthropic Claude models, opencode.
How is your project creative?

One of the greatest challenges our team faced was to find a way to interlink education and the agriculture solution, in a way that wasn't only related, but actually natural and dependent on each other. After lots of brainstorming, the answer was actually quite obvious. Older generations usually aren't great at using technology, which limits them from using it. On the other hand, the youth is naturally adept with it. Therefore, we focused the project on teaching that same youth, so that they could later teach their farmer parents and grandparents, and learn from them. This would contribute to both the present and future of the problematic.

What factors did your team consider?

Our main users are high school and college students, especially young people from agricultural communities in Chihuahua. That shaped most of our decisions: results are written in plain language, variables are defined simply, and the interface follows a “detective” flow (pick a variable, pick a place, read the answer) instead of showing raw statistical output.
